newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Options for Milosevic in battle for Belgrade.
newsitem.headline: Options for Milosevic in battle for Belgrade.

text.p: Three weeks of street protests, court appeals and Western coaxing have failed to swing the battle between President Slobodan Milosevic and his reborn opposition over who controls Serbia's cities.
The supreme court at the weekend denied the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition's claim that it was cheated of victory in November 17 local elections by Milosevic's ruling socialists.
The verdict should have exhausted the legal avenues open to Zajedno which has waged a parallel campaign of marches and rallies in Belgrade that mobilise up to 150,000 people a day.
But up popped the city election commission to tantalise the opposition with the prospect that Belgrade, the election jewel, was not definitively lost.
It proposed another appeal to the Yugoslav federal public prosecutor and supreme court.

That will take time, which Milosevic needs in his struggle to maintain 50 years of unbroken socialist power in Serbia where the formerly communist ruling party has changed its name but not its ideology.
Political sources say the Serbian leader has three basic options.

He can let loose the police and army which, the United States has warned, would outrage the West. He can string the conflict out, hoping the mainly student and middle class demonstrators will tire. Or he can surrender the cities and make sure the untried opposition make a mess of running them.
Milosevic has refrained from force, aware perhaps that many rank-and-file police are as disgruntled as the rest of the impoverished population about Serbia's social and economic plight.
There is no sign, however, that he is ready for compromise if the game can be won.

American media rights worker Kati Marton, who met Milosevic on Saturday, said: "I think he feels he has support from the countryside so he can ride it out. I don't think he is in a mood to give up. Not at all."

The opposition's dilemma is to keep momentum. Its protests are big and sustained but have not attracted the support of workers to broaden its intelligentsia class-base. Threatened strikes by workers, which could shake the government, have not happened.
The federal appeal process gives Milosevic a breathing space of up to a week to see whether street support for Zajedno starts to crumble.
If it does not, political sources say, he could bow to option three, letting opposition mayors take control of Belgrade and some or all of the 14 other cities Zajedno claims to have won.
"Milosevic thinks that Belgrade is a plane that (Zajedno leader) Vuk (Draskovic) cannot fly," a Belgrade daily said.
It would be relatively easy for the state-controlled media to smear Zajedno with responsibility for the broken-down city services they will inherit wherever they take over.
In Belgrade, transport, hospitals and other essential services have been reduced to chaos by the country's economic dislocation. As winter bites the situation can only get worse.
Political sources thought this was Milosevic's strategy when the socialists at first accepted Zajedno had won in Belgrade.

Discredited opposition management of the cities would give the socialists powerful propaganda during Serbian republican elections next year, the outcome of which will be crucial to Milosevic's grip on power for the next decade.
This may still happen, but his electoral credibility has taken a battering now that the opposition has succeeded in making charges of election rigging stick.
Zajedno is suspicious of the sincerity of Western support it has received despite trenchant U.S. criticism of Milosevic and demands for democratic progress.

Stability in Serbia is crucial to Balkan security. For as long as Milosevic is demonstrably in control, he may be more preferable to the West than the unknown, quarrelsome Zajedno leaders who have never held power.

For Milosevic's bedrock supporters among pensioners, workers and country dwellers, socialist rule is a way of life they have always known in a society largely comfortable with authoritarian government.
In the provinces, thanks to Milosevic's control of the media, many people do not even know of the battle for Belgrade.
